rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation guidance for Jabberwocky words (Carroll's Preface)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll gives explicit pronunciations: 'slithy' — the 'i' is long as in 'writhe'; 'toves' pronounced to rhyme with 'groves'; the first 'o' in 'borogoves' is pronounced like the 'o' in 'borrow'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notes are Carroll’s prescriptions for how to read certain nonce words from the related poem 'Jabberwocky' to the audience; he also notes common mispronunciations as 'Human Perversity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Humpty-Dumpty portmanteau explanation for invented words (Carroll's Preface)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humpty-Dumpty's theory: two meanings packed into one word like a portmanteau. Example given: combine 'fuming' and 'furious' by intending to say both but leaving order unsettled to produce 'frumious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carroll offers this as the right explanation for many 'hard words' in his earlier poem, demonstrating a playful method for coinage that affects pronunciation and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical maxim: 'What I tell you three times is true' (Bellman's speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bellman asserts that repeating something three times makes it true: 'Just the place for a Snark! I have said it twice: ... I have said it thrice: What I tell you three times is true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a comic/satirical rule for persuading the crew; functions as a rhetorical device (repetition) within the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bellman's 'five unmistakable marks' of a genuine Snark (Fit the Second)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bellman lists five marks by which you may know a warranted genuine Snark: (1) its taste — meagre and hollow but crisp; (2) habit of getting up late (frequently breakfasts at five-o'clock tea and dines the following day); (3) slowness in taking a jest — sighs and looks grave at a pun; (4) fondness for bathing-machines which it constantly carries about; (5) ambition — distinguishing batches: those that have feathers and bite, and those that have whiskers and scratch. He adds a warning that some Snarks are Boojums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are whimsical identification criteria for an imaginary creature (a poetic device) rather than objective biological taxonomy; they function as literary features that characterize the poem's nonsense world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested (comic) methods for hunting/capturing a Snark (repeated refrain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated instructions in the poem: 'seek it with thimbles', 'pursue it with forks and hope', 'threaten its life with a railway-share', 'charm it with smiles and soap' — presented as the Bellman's exhortations for the hunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are absurd, humorous 'procedural' prescriptions inside the poem; they serve as running motifs and satirize earnest manuals or hunt instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable authority and literal rule-following (Preface/poem satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll satirizes blind adherence to rules and manuals (e.g., the bowsprit being revarnished and reattached wrongly because nobody could interpret the Bellman's Admiralty Instructions; Rule 42 'No one shall speak to the Man at the Helm' completed by 'and the Man at the Helm shall speak to no one'), illustrating how procedural formalities can produce absurd outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a critical theme rather than a prescriptive rubric for producing text; it highlights the comedic value of bureaucratic literalism.
